paper_design_summary: An online experiment analyzed 905 Prolific participants across analytical, ethical and creative tasks, with triads randomly assigned to human-only or hybrid teams containing undisclosed supportive or contrarian AI teammates (pp. 2-6). Blinded trained researchers scored individual movie plots before and after discussion for originality, elaboration and coherence, and separately scored creative-task chat transcripts for discussion quality (pp. 9-13 and 33). An independent pilot with 15 people assessed AI humanness and reported no human creative-output outcome (p. 8).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly formed into triads, and triads were randomly assigned to human-only versus hybrid compositions with supportive, contrarian or mixed AI personas. Each participant completed one task domain; the factorial design crossed task with condition. AI involvement was undisclosed. Allocation mechanisms and allocation-stage counts are not specified (p. 2; pp. 4-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2).

participants.exclusions: The paper says 1,047 initially entered, not that 1,047 were randomized. Excluded: attention-check failure n = 36; inadequate discussion engagement n = 67 (fewer than five messages and average message length below 20 characters); incomplete post-task survey n = 20; mismatch between individual and discussion task n = 19 (pp. 3-4, section 3.1). Primary analyses retain 905 people in 572 groups. A further 34 people with display-name mismatches are omitted only from BDI-related analyses, leaving 871 people; they remain in other analyses (p. 4). Table 2 is recorded as analyzed task-by-condition counts, not pre-exclusion randomization counts. No intention-to-treat analysis is claimed.
participants.who: English-fluent adult Prolific participants, recruited between 21 August 2025 and 20 September 2025. Stated eligibility age range is 18-65; Table 1 nevertheless includes a 65+ category. The 905-person count describes the entire main experiment, not just the creative-writing task (pp. 3-4, Section 3.1 and Table 1).

ai_tool.how_used: Generative conversational agents acted as undisclosed teammates in synchronous group chat, using supportive or contrarian system prompts (pp. 5, 7-8, sections 3.2 and 3.4-3.5; pp. 29-31, Appendix B). They contributed and responded to the developing discussion under probabilistic scheduling and turn-taking constraints. This is social participation by an AI teammate, not a comparison of standalone AI and human stories. The document does not identify the underlying model, provider, version or sampling settings.

task.description: The eligible task was movie-plot brainstorming: develop characters, setting, key events and resolution, with AGI central to a plot beginning 'In the year 2045, the world's first AGI unexpectedly...' (p. 28, Appendix A.3; p. 7, section 3.3). Participants produced baseline and post-discussion individual responses around a group ideation phase (pp. 5-6). Other randomized task domains were survival-item ranking and an autonomous-vehicle moral dilemma (pp. 6-7, 26-28). They are part of the same experiment but are not scored as creative-writing outcomes here.
task.duration: Group discussion lasted 10 minutes (p. 5, section 3.2; p. 6, Figure 2). Individual pre/post writing durations and total session duration are not stated.

outcomes.name: Creative-writing individual performance gain (composite)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Creative-task component of the paper's standardized individual performance gain. Two independent researchers trained in education and psychology, blinded to condition, scored pre- and post-discussion stories; final ratings were averaged across raters (pp. 9-10, section 3.7). The story rubric comprises originality, elaboration, and coherence, each scored 1-5 (p. 33, Table 9); Table 6 reports a total score (p. 11). Gain is post-task minus baseline and continuous outcomes were standardized before analysis (p. 11, section 3.9). The precise total-score aggregation and standardization reference population are not fully specified. The primary LMM pools all tasks, includes Task x Condition and a group random intercept, and reports group-clustered CR2 inference with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and Holm adjustment (pp. 12-13, section 3.11; p. 52, Table 28). Creative is the reference task, so condition main effects in Table 28 are creative-task contrasts, not effects averaged over tasks. Table 29 gives estimated marginal means and their own SEs/CIs, not raw arm means/SDs (p. 53). Conventional LMM inference, BDI-adjusted models/EMMs (pp. 54-55, Tables 31-32), and BDI moderation (pp. 56-58, Table 34 and section G.6) are variants of this outcome. Full moderation EMMs and simple contrasts are relegated to external XLSX files. Phase C repeats the task individually after AI-containing discussion, so this is immediate after_ai, not a delayed transfer test (pp. 5-6).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2); no later-session follow-up.

outcomes.name: Creative-story originality (post-discussion; baseline also rated)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: One of the creative-writing rubric dimensions, rated 1-5 for novelty, surprising combinations and freedom from predictable genre conventions (p. 33, Table 9). Two trained education/psychology researchers independently rated submissions, blinded to condition (pp. 9-10, section 3.7). Measured at baseline and post-discussion; Table 6 reports inter-rater reliability only for the separate dimension (p. 11). No arm-level originality means, SDs or treatment contrasts are printed. The dimension contributes to S1-O1; an absent subscale effect is not coded as a null finding. The scored post-discussion story is individually produced in Phase C (pp. 5-6). Unit is participant, following the paper's individual-level classification of pre/post rubric performance (p. 11, section 3.9); each participant supplies an individual task response in each phase. The paper supplies no separate component-effect model.

outcomes.name: Group discussion quality during creative ideation (composite)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert-coded quality of the creative-task chat transcript, comprising idea generation and sharing, collaborative engagement, and progression and synthesis; each dimension is rated 1-5 (p. 33, Table 8). The two blinded education/psychology researchers rated the transcripts, with ratings averaged across raters (pp. 9-10, section 3.7); dimension ratings were averaged to a group composite (pp. 11-12, section 3.9). This evaluates observable ideation and collaboration processes, not the originality of a final story, and is retained separately from the core creativity score. The full Task x Condition OLS has one observation per group; n_units refers to the pooled model across all tasks, not solely Creative (pp. 12-13; p. 47, Table 24). Listed contrasts are for Creative, the reference task. CR2 inference and Holm adjustment are used for directions. Estimated marginal means in Table 25 have separately reported SEs and CIs (p. 48). BDI-adjusted models (pp. 49-50, Tables 26-27), exploratory BDI simple contrasts (p. 57, Table 37), and linguistic mediation (pp. 59-64, Appendix H) are variants of the same discussion-quality measure. AI agents are active in Phase B while the transcript is produced (pp. 5-6). Reconciliation retains this transcript-scored creative-ideation outcome under other, together with its components. Its rubric evaluates the sharing, development and synthesis of ideas during the creative task; it is not an overall-creativity score for the final story and does not independently establish eligibility criterion 3. It compares group interaction quality, not similarity between different people's outputs.
outcomes.delay: During the group discussion (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2).

studies.label: Independent pilot: perceived humanness of AI teammate scheduling

assignment.what_was_assigned: Every pilot participant interacted with two AI teammates under the same selected scheduling protocol. No allocation among experimental conditions or treatment order is reported. Repeated humanness ratings of two teammates do not establish a within-person treatment design; assignment unit is coded other (no reported assignment contrast), and structure is null (not applicable to the reported single-protocol validation).

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria. The paper explicitly reports random assignment of triads to human-only or generative-AI teammate conditions during their own collaborative tasks (PDF p. 2, Introduction; pp. 4-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2). The main experiment analyzed 905 people after exclusions (pp. 3-4, section 3.1); the creative-writing arms alone exceed the people threshold, with analyzed counts of H3 = 90, H2_C = 62, H2_S = 57, H1_C = 30, H1_S = 29 and H1_M = 30 (p. 6, Table 2). Two blinded trained researchers scored participants' movie-plot submissions for originality, elaboration and coherence (pp. 9-11, sections 3.7 and 3.9; p. 33, Table 9), with creative-task gain contrasts printed in Table 28 (p. 52). Phase C submissions were produced individually after the AI-containing discussion, supporting immediate after_ai coding (pp. 5-6, section 3.2 and Figure 2). H3 supplies human partners, so AI-versus-H3 comparisons are ai_vs_active. The separate pilot analyzed 15 people and measured perceived AI humanness only, so it does not qualify independently (p. 8, section 3.5). None of the remaining reporting gaps affects these eligibility findings.

one_line_finding: Following the discussion, creative-writing gains showed no clear advantage from AI teammates: H2_S versus H3 beta = 0.336, CR2 SE = 0.184, p = .074, Holm p = 1.00; the other creative AI-versus-H3 contrasts also had Holm p = 1.00 (p. 52, Table 28).
open_questions: The underlying generative model, provider, version and sampling settings are not identified in the implementation sections or persona prompts (pp. 7-8 and 29-31).
The coded-exemplar supplementary dataset and external XLSX moderation outputs are named without an access URL (p. 10; pp. 56-58). They are not included in the supplied PDF.

The exact aggregation of creative-writing rubric dimensions and the reference population/denominator for gain standardization are not fully specified (pp. 9-13 and 51-55). Raw arm means/SDs and separate treatment effects for originality, elaboration, coherence and discussion components are not printed.

Methods define BDI as Balanced Detection Index (pp. 10-11), but Appendices E and G call it baseline depression or depressive symptoms (pp. 38 and 56). The correct moderator interpretation requires clarification; the primary estimates do not condition on BDI.

Table 37 prints the same exploratory discussion-quality contrast, 3.52 (SE 0.12), for every task and both BDI levels (p. 57). The transcription is confirmed, but the repeated values and their scale cannot be independently checked without SI_GDQ_CR2_BDI_CR2.xlsx or author clarification.

open_items.item: The underlying generative model, provider, version and sampling settings are not identified (pp. 7-8, sections 3.4-3.5; pp. 29-31, Appendix B). Author-supplied implementation details would settle this. Criterion 1 is already met by the documented generative-AI teammate intervention and random assignment; a model identifier is not needed to establish it.

The coded-exemplar supplementary dataset and external XLSX moderation outputs are named without an access URL and are absent from the supplied PDF (p. 10, section 3.7; pp. 56-58, Appendix G). Obtaining those supplements would settle their contents and availability. The PDF itself establishes assignment, analyzed people counts and scored creative outputs, so no eligibility criterion depends on them.

The exact aggregation of creative-writing rubric dimensions and the reference population/denominator for standardizing performance gain remain unspecified (pp. 9-13, sections 3.7-3.11; pp. 51-55, Appendix F). The authors' scoring and standardization specification would settle this. Criterion 3 is met because originality, elaboration and coherence are scored on participants' submissions regardless of the unresolved aggregation details.

Raw arm means/SDs and separate treatment effects for originality, elaboration, coherence and discussion components are not printed (p. 11, Table 6; p. 33, Tables 8-9; pp. 47-55, Tables 24-33). Posted participant/group-level ratings with task, condition, phase and group identifiers would permit their recovery. These missing extraction statistics do not affect any eligibility criterion; the PDF reports qualifying output scores and composite contrasts.

Methods define BDI as Balanced Detection Index (pp. 10-11, section 3.8), while Appendix E calls it baseline depression (p. 38) and Appendix G calls it baseline depressive symptoms (p. 56). Authors must confirm the variable used in the adjusted/moderation analyses. No eligibility criterion depends on this discrepancy, and the primary creative-performance model does not condition on BDI (p. 52, Table 28).

Table 37 prints the exploratory H2_S minus H2_C discussion-quality estimate as 3.52 (SE 0.12) for every task and both BDI levels (p. 57). Its transcription is confirmed, but its repeated values and scale remain unverified. SI_GDQ_CR2_BDI_CR2.xlsx, named in section G.5, is needed to check the intended estimates. This secondary reporting issue does not affect eligibility, which is independently established by the individual movie-plot scores.
